read: full: main text pp. 1-9 (abstract, introduction, related work, experimental setup, automatic evaluation, crowdsourced and in-house human evaluation, plagiarism study, discussion, conclusion, limitations); appendices skimmed (inter-annotator agreement, pp. 15-16)
venue_now: INLG 2023 (Proceedings of the 16th International Natural Language Generation Conference), pp. 323-351 (page 1 header)
what_it_is: An empirical study of open-ended story generation that compares GPT-3 (text-davinci-001, prompted with 2 or 3 example stories) with five other story generators (KGGPT2, PROGEN, MTCL, HINT, BART) on ROCStories, WritingPrompts and CNN news stories (pp. 2-4, Table 1). Stories are scored with reference-based and reference-free automatic metrics and by human raters (Mechanical Turk crowdworkers and in-house judges) on fluency, coherence, relatedness, logicality and interestingness, on a 1-5 scale (pp. 3-6). It finds GPT-3's stories better than the other models' and comparable to human-written ones, that lexical metrics agree weakly with human ratings, and that GPT-3 sometimes reproduces real stories: 7 of 10 sampled CNN stories were based on real news (pp. 1, 6-8).
domain: story generation (creative natural language generation); no reasoning or engineering content
size: 3 story datasets; GPT-3 plus 5 comparison models; automatic metrics on 800 (ROC), 1,000 (WP) and 600 (CNN) generated stories (p. 3); human evaluation on 20 sampled contexts per dataset per annotator group, 3 raters per story (pp. 5-6)
source_of_items: existing story datasets (ROCStories, WritingPrompts, CNN); conditioning contexts sampled from their test splits (p. 3)
instances: n/a (evaluation study; the stories are generated by the compared models from sampled contexts)
evaluation: reference-based metrics (corpus BLEU, MS-Jaccard, BERTScore, BLEURT, backward BLEU) and reference-free metrics (diversity, BARTScore, length) (pp. 3-4), plus human ratings of five aspects on a 1-5 ordinal scale (pp. 5-6)
human_validation: human ratings from Mechanical Turk workers and 15 in-house raters (14 PhD students and 1 staff member), 3 raters per story (pp. 5-6); agreement reported as one-vs-rest Pearson r, with 9 strong (r >= 0.6) and 6 moderate results for the crowdworkers (pp. 15-16)
contamination_measures: none as a design measure; it probes memorisation after the fact with iThenticate (similarity 4%, 3% and 14% for ROC, WP and CNN) and a manual check of 10 stories each for WP and CNN (p. 7)

engtrace_use.sentence: As LLMs expand into high-stakes engineering workflows, rigorous evaluation of their reasoning capabilities has become paramount (Zhao et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2023a). (Introduction, L45-48)
engtrace_use.explanation: The paper studies GPT-3 story generation and how to evaluate stories (pp. 1-9). It does not discuss reasoning evaluation, engineering or high-stakes deployment, so it gives no support to the claim that rigorous evaluation of LLM reasoning has become paramount as LLMs enter high-stakes engineering workflows. Its nearest points are that automatic lexical metrics correlate weakly with human evaluation (p. 8) and that 'the question of circularity, i.e. using LLMs to evaluate LLM-generated text, will be the next challenge' (p. 9); neither concerns reasoning or engineering. Cited beside Zhao et al. as support for the opening premise, it suggests support the paper does not give. Zhuohan Xie is first author here and an EngTrace author (citation map C9), so an unsupported self-citation in the first sentence of the paper is a likely reviewer complaint.

suggested_wording: None for the Introduction. If the paper ever needs it, the accurate use is narrow: in story generation, human raters judged GPT-3's stories comparable to human-written ones, while automatic lexical metrics agreed weakly with their ratings (Xie et al., 2023a).
facts_to_cite: Compares GPT-3 (text-davinci-001, prompt-based) with five story-generation models on ROCStories, WritingPrompts and CNN (pp. 2-4, Table 1).
Human raters, both crowdworkers and in-house judges, rated GPT-3's stories above those of the other models and comparable to human-written stories (pp. 1, 6, 8).
Automatic lexical metrics correlate weakly with human evaluation, and model-based metrics appear more reliable (p. 8).
7 of 10 sampled GPT-3 CNN stories were based on real news stories, with most details faithful to the originals (p. 7).
The authors expect circularity, using LLMs to evaluate LLM-generated text, to be the field's next challenge (p. 9).
overlap_with_engtrace: None of substance. It shares an interest in checking automatic evaluation against human judgement (p. 8), but it has no generated instances, no gold traces, no step-level evaluation, no engineering domain and no expert validation of an evaluator; its raters are crowdworkers and students judging story quality, not correctness (pp. 5-6).
notes: Self-citation (citation map C9). The May reference matches the INLG version (pp. 323-351). The DeltaScore paper (xie2023deltascore) reuses this study's stories and human ratings (DeltaScore p. 4; its reference list, p. 11), so the two self-citations stand or fall together. The p. 9 remark on LLM-judge circularity is too slight to earn a place in the planned judge-validity paragraph.
